Artificial intelligence represents an entirely new paradigm. And it will develop rapidly, perhaps faster than any of us realise. To be precise, we must shape AI, because otherwise AI will shape us. We must embed, as a first principle, safety by design. Rules of conduct and respect for human values, and that this technology is accessible to everyone, that it does not allow dangerous misuse and is never directed against humans. We need clear guidance towards positive value and use for humanity. That is why Germany warmly welcomes this global dialogue at UN level. Our discussions built on important foundations. The OECD AI Principles, UNESCO's Ethics Recommendation, and ITU's AI for Good platform. For Germany, a multi-stakeholder approach is a necessity. Industry, academia, and civil society, especially from underrepresented regions, must have a meaningful seat at the table. Germany will also establish a national AI safety and security institute anchored in cutting-edge research and plugged into European and international networks. This dialogue is a unique moment, and a successful first global dialogue can lay the foundation for greater international cooperation on AI, which is truly needed in a fast evolving AI landscape. Today, frontier AI is reaching capabilities that were simply unimaginable before, and even a few weeks ago were not imaginable. This is opening extraordinary opportunities for innovation and for improving quality of life. And this is happening in biotechnology, for example. AI is accelerating the design of new proteins and new drugs. In Europe, we welcome these advances and we are investing to make them possible. We will upgrade our unique network of public supercomputers and AI factories and gigafactories. We are expanding Eurocompute capacity, offering this to scientists and startups. And we do this also with the recent European law, which is called the AI and Cloud Development Act. Because we believe AI will be the defining driver of Europe's future prosperity and competitiveness. And we promote an AI-first approach. From industrial AI to physical AI and advanced robotics, these technologies are creating an entirely new competition and societal paradigm. However, this fast evolution also carries considerable societal risks. While AI can equip children with valuable skills and open new horizons for learning, it also can be used to manipulate, exploit, and harm them. Similarly, AI can be very efficient for power grids, but also also offer criminals the possibility to actually damage them. The tension between transformation and opportunities and new risks defines the central challenge before us in this meeting and in this dialogue. It brings me to what we are discussing today: how to best govern AI. The EU has adopted the approach of responsible and trustworthy AI innovation. We support the development and the development of safe and secure sustainable AI. Our approach is both human-centric and grounded on international human rights. With this objective, the EU has adopted uniform risk-based rules across our single market. Our legislation only intervenes when the risk is too high or unacceptable. Based on this experience, we want to contribute to the conversation globally. Governance should be informed by facts and evidence. This is why the EU places particular importance on the work of the independent International Scientific Panel on AI, whose preliminary findings have already made a contribution to this dialogue. The dialogue is our chance to clarify the opportunities and risks of AI, and to develop ideas for concrete solutions that contribute to making safe, trustworthy, inclusive, sustainable, and widely accessible AI a reality. It is also the opportunity to discuss regional needs and specificities, and share workable solutions. Excellencies, the EU comes to this dialogue seeking something durable, a shared commitment to the principle that technology and its benefits must serve all humanity and the planet, and leaving no one behind. The EU has substantial practice in developing governance in this field and is ready to share its experience and, of course, to learn from all of you. And we come with the intellectual honesty to say we don't know everything. This is precisely why evidence, multi-stakeholder dialogue, and multilateralism are needed at this very moment. Thank you for your attention.

I thank His Excellency Roberto Viola, Director-General, European Commission, speaking on behalf of the EU and its member states. Next speaker is His Excellency Haliki Choua Mohamed, Minister of Telecommunications, Digital Economy, and Digitalization of Public Administration from Chad.

I thank His Excellency Haleki Tchoua Mahamat, Minister of Telecommunications, Digital Economy, and Digitalization of Public Administration of Chad. Next speaker is His Excellency Chai Chanok Chitchop, Minister of Digital Economy and Society of Thailand.

I thank His Excellency Chai Chanok Chitchop, Minister of Digital Digital Economy and Society of Thailand. Next speaker is Her Excellency Meotia Viada Hafid, Minister of Communications and Digital Affairs of Indonesia.

On the map of global technology, the Maldives is easy to overlook, but we are not here to be a footnote. We are here because the future being designed in rooms like this will be judged by whether it works for countries like ours. And for many small islands and developing states who share our reality. For countries like ours, AI is not a race for prestige. It is a tool for public problem-solving. Its value lies not in novelty, but in whether it helps us serve people better and extend people more fairly. For a nation like ours, that means one thing above all: the quality of a citizen's service should never depend on how far they live from the capital. That is why, under Maldives 2.0 roadmap, we treat AI as one layer within a broader transformation. It must rest on digital public infrastructure, trusted data, cybersecurity, and clear accountability. For us, inclusion begins with that foundation, because without AI deepens inequality rather than reducing it, concentrating benefits in already capable institutions and leaving others further behind. So when we speak of AI for all, we must be honest about what for all requires: digital foundations that are not fragmented, institutions that can govern AI with confidence and local capability rather than permanent dependency. The Maldives has grounded this action— this in action. With UNESCO, we completed South Asia's first national AI readiness assessment, and we have established our national AI and data competency center, the Maldives AI Lab, to move from fragmented experimentation towards coordinated, governed capability across government. From our experience, 3 priorities deserve emphasis. First, invest in foundations, not only applications. AI cannot compete or cannot compensate for weak data systems or thin institutional capacity. Third, treat interoperability as a governance principle. It lets countries build incrementally and adapt new tools on a stable, sovereign foundation. Excellencies, the future of AI governance will not be measured by the sophistication of the most advanced systems. Thank you.

Co-chairs, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, a very good afternoon. It is an honor to address this inaugural Global Dialogue on behalf of the Prime Minister of Pakistan. I commend the co-chairs and the United Nations, ITU, and UNESCO for bringing us to this moment. The theme of this segment, Harnessing the Benefits of AI for All, is exactly right. Pakistan comes to this plenary with clear vision. For all can be achieved if this dialogue continues to confront structural imbalances head-on. The capability divide is real and it is widening.

Much of the Global South faces deficits in energy, broadband, data centers, high-performance compute, and AI talent.

Foundational models are built and controlled elsewhere. Left to drift, the benefits concentrate where capability already sits, while the risks of job displacement, biased systems, extracting of data for value generation, and new dependencies fall on those least able to absorb them. So let me be direct about what inclusion must mean. First, inclusion is a voice in writing the rules. Norms, standards, and interoperability frameworks must be authored by both those already at the summit and those who've just started climbing. Every nation should chart its own AI path in line with its own history, languages, and development priorities while honoring international consensus. Every child must grow in a safe environment firmly rooted in their cultural values and social identities while developing knowledge, skills, and perspective to thrive in the global world. Today, secondly, we feel that inclusion without investment is an empty promise.

Pakistan calls for concrete resource mechanisms, access to open-source models, shared compute initiatives, support for data infrastructure, and national AI strategies, regulatory sandboxes fit for local conditions, and South-South and South-East-West cooperation.

All of these to be anchored explicitly in the Sustainable Development Goals, because the whole purpose of governance is to enable development. We must also effectively advance the consideration of the proposed Global Fund for AI. Pakistan is doing its part. Our national AI policy ensures human in the loop where AI must support and not replace human decision-making. Human on the loop, where human oversight remains an inbuilt feature. And human in command, where ultimate legal responsibility remains that of humans. It is also rooted in ethical AI principles where fairness, transparency, accountability, safety, and inclusivity are at the center of any AI deployment. Our upcoming National Data Governance Policy treats data as a national asset held in trust of our people with federated custody, governed exchange, citizen empowerment, and risk-tiered controls with meaningful human oversight. It is sovereignty by default.

Distinguished colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, thank you and good afternoon. AI represents a potentially transformational shift in humanity's relationship to technology, accelerating scientific discovery innovation, and economic growth. The question before us is whether we will create the conditions to ensure AI development and deployment benefits our respective citizens and preserves their liberty and way of life. As AI empowers breakthroughs in medicine, manufacturing, education, and energy, it lays the foundations for new industries and new ways for individuals to amplify their personal creative capacities. These transformative benefits will only be realized through widespread adoption. Governments can play an important role in accelerating AI adoption in 2 ways. First, governments are key adopters themselves and can act as examples for effective employment of AI, improving the services they provide their citizens. Second, governments can help to establish trust in these technologies and competence and accountability for their misapplication. The Trump administration is working with American legislators as they construct a national policy framework for AI that protects children, prevents censorship, respects intellectual property, and supports our workers, families, and our communities. Combined with a pro-innovation environment that allows AI companies to meet people's real needs. The framework will assure the public that these tools and its infrastructure can benefit their lives. Government has an essential role to play in building public trust, but it cannot do this alone. As AI capabilities continue to advance, industry must be a core partner in AI security. Industry is intimately aware of the state, scope, trajectory of AI developments. Government is not. Voluntary cooperation between the two is the only AI security approach agile enough to meet challenges as they arise without stifling innovation. American companies are leading the world in advancing the reliability, robustness, and security of AI systems, and the Trump administration is passionate about sharing the benefits of American AI with the rest of the world. Our hope is that shared efforts to to advance the diffusion of the full AI stack across partner countries will become an occasion for bilateral diplomacy, international development, and global economic dynamism. We are working hard to make sure that the AI future is one of prosperous collaboration and peaceful competition around the world. America has been the dynamic center of global science and technology and the world leader in AI development because our This experiment in self-government gives innovators the freedom to discover and build the next frontier. We invite you to join us in fostering—

I thank the distinguished high-level representative of the United States of America, and now I give the floor to the Minister for Digital Development and Information of Singapore, Her Excellency Josephine Teo.

Co-chairs, colleagues, and friends, thank you for coming together to discuss a very important topic. By now, many countries have some experience promoting AI adoption. Let me share what Singapore has learned from a governance perspective. The first lesson is that we need a few building blocks to achieve our AI goals for the economy and society. One, reliable infrastructure, including the software layer that makes AI accessible and useful. 2, access to quality data. Among the 11 states of ASEAN, we have established a Digital Economy Framework Agreement to develop common rules and interoperable standards to support cross-border data flow. 3, capabilities— people and organizations that know how to use AI confidently, maximizing its upsides and minimizing its downsides. The second lesson is the need to build trust, because people will not use a technology they do not trust. For example, Singapore has published guidelines on the responsible use of data, for AI models and on AI agents. We update our laws to deal with AI risks. We also partner international bodies like the ISO and IEC to standardise the methodology for testing generative AI systems. But it's important to recognise that so much is still unknown about AI risks. Singapore has therefore hosted the international scientific exchange for AI safety experts from academia, industry, and civic organisations, who have in turn developed the Singapore Consensus for AI Safety Research Priorities. The third lesson is that AI can be a significant force for good. The government itself can use AI to be more efficient, and effective when delivering public services. But whether in the public or private sectors, it takes more than big bang announcements and high-profile projects. It is more like the patient work of tending a garden, sowing seeds and removing weeds before the flowers bloom. The Global Dialogue on AI Governance and other platforms can be a community of AI gardeners, growing each member state's capacity for vibrant yet safe AI ecosystems. Singapore will remain committed to doing our part so that the benefits of AI can be enjoyed by the many and not the few. Thank you.

I thank the distinguished Minister for Digital Development and Information of Singapore. And now I give the floor to the Minister of State with responsibility for trade promotion, artificial intelligence, and digital transformation of Ireland, Her Excellency Niamh Smith.

This global dialogue marks a critical step in our collective efforts to to implement these agreements and to move forward with a balanced, inclusive, risk-based approach to AI governance, one that aims to harness the potential for safe, secure, and trustworthy AI to change the world for the better, one that improves our capacity to deal with its consequences, visible and those less visible. This dialogue can facilitate much-needed efforts towards shared governance language incorporating transparency, accountability, and oversight, and it can advance multi-stakeholder cooperation towards safe and equitable access to AI technologies. The work ahead requires sustained political will and genuine collaboration. The progress made here can be sustained with practical outcomes and follow-up, ensuring a collective response is to share— is a shared challenge. Go raibh míle maith agat, and thank you everyone.

Backed by the incentives and infrastructure required to draw both local startups and international AI players to our shores. We cannot allow the digital divide to harden into an AI divide. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished Minister of State for Information, Communications, Technology, and National Guidance of Uganda. I thank the distinguished Minister for the Indo-Pacific and Minister for Equalities of the UK, and I give the floor to the Minister of Communications and Digital Transformation of Mozambique, His Excellency Américo Muchanga.

Excellencies, it is a privilege for the Republic of Mozambique to participate in this high-level dialogue on artificial intelligence. AI is redefining the global landscape at a speed not seen before. Like every transformative technology before it, AI will shape economies, power, opportunity, security, and human development for generations to come. The question before us is not whether AI will transform our societies; it is whether that transformation will be fair, inclusive, and guided by our shared values. For Mozambique, AI is a strategic enabler for sustainable development, and for that, we are developing a national strategy of AI. We would like to apply it to strengthen agricultural productivity, improve healthcare delivery, enhance education, reinforce climate resilience, support disaster readiness, modernize public administration, and expand opportunities for millions of our citizens. However, we must recognize a fundamental reality: if access to AI remains concentrated among few countries and a handful of corporations, we risk creating a technological divide that will leave developing countries further behind. Mozambique therefore calls for a global AI ecosystem founded on 3 essential pillars. First, inclusive governance. It demands investment in digital infrastructure, affordable connectivity, reliable energy, quality education, digital literacy, research innovation, and development of local talent. Third, trust. AI must remain firmly anchored in human dignity, transparency, accountability, respect for human rights, cybersecurity, and international law. History will judge our generation not by how quickly we developed AI, but how wisely we governed it. The decisions we make today will tell whether AI becomes a force that narrows inequalities or widens them, that empowers humanity or concentrates opportunity in the hands of a few. Mozambique stands ready to work with all member states and partners to build an AI future that's open, secure, inclusive, and open-centered. Let us ensure that AI becomes not a privilege of few, but a shared asset for all humanity. Because the future does not belong to those who possess the most powerful algorithms, it belongs to those who ensure the innovation, serves humanity dignity and fairness and hope. With that, I thank you all.

They have ideas.

Good day, one and all. Co-chairs, good day. And this is a determining issue for economic, social, and political issues of all nations. The South countries, countries of the Global South, must have a sovereign right to collect, store, and analyze their data. It's not just a protectionist aspect that I'm saying here. No, it's a matter of the dignity and the sovereignty of each nation at an international level. The non-neutrality of AI also— AI is not neutral. It actually reflects the biases of those who are doing the training. So AI systems which are based on non-representative data can amplify discrimination, worsen discrimination even. The challenges which inhibit the participation of countries such as Mali in this revolution of AI are as follows. First of all, an insufficiency of our infrastructures and skills. Without reliable electricity, without a fast internet connection, we can't have AI, for example. With regard to skills, they're of course concentrated in higher capitals of different countries. AI is a question of emergence Sub-Saharan African countries are underrepresented in this space. Insecurity is, of course, impacting development in all countries of the Sahel group. This— their participation is a prerequisite for any investment in any technology of the future. Ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of the transitional government and the people of Mali, we would like to make the following recommendations. First of all, the adoption of an international framework for AI governance which respects all and which has clear international rules respecting the rights of developing countries and the sovereign rights of countries to equitably be represented in their data, amongst other things. Also, a dedicated space in the development area which is focused on least developed countries. Also, we need to represent African languages and cultures in AI. Thank you very much for your kind attention.
Merci, Monsieur le Ministre. Thank you, Minister, from Mali. Now I give the floor to the Secretary of State for Innovation of Italy, His Excellency Alessio Butti.

Distinguished colleagues, dear co-chairs, the question today is no longer whether AI will change our societies. It already is. The question is whether we will manage to govern it or end up being governed by it. I thank the United Nations for convening the first Global Dialogue on AI Governance, which we truly hope could provide substantial guidance to parallel and sectorial ongoing dialogue initiatives. A challenge of this magnitude requires principles, that are truly universal and shared by all, not imposed by the few, and that every country can then adapt to its own governance experience. For too long, we have treated artificial intelligence as something to watch unfold. It is time we treated it as a responsibility to share. For Italy, governance of this kind means first and foremost Putting the person at the center. Safety, reliability, transparency of the underlying algorithms and datasets that reflect the plurality of the world's languages and cultures, not just a few of them. It also means designing artificial intelligence according to a security-by-design approach, because trust in these systems is built by preventing malicious uses not by chasing after them. It means involving all stakeholders— governments, businesses, civil society, the research community— because no one can write these rules alone. And above all, it means closing the existing digital divide without opening a new one— the AI divide. The concentration of these technologies in a few companies and a few countries is a risk for everyone. Not only for those left out. Italy brings to this dialogue a concrete experience as well. Our law on artificial intelligence aligns our national legal framework with the European AI Act and entrusts governance of the sector to 2 existing agencies. The rules we build together are not a brake on innovation. They are the guardrail that makes it safer and faster. Thank you, and count on Italy as a strong supporter of the EU and efforts to shape AI governance globally. Thank you.
Thank you, Secretary of State of Italy. Now I give the floor to the Minister for the Digital Economy and Sovereignty of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, Her Excellency

The Netherlands strongly supports the establishment of this dialogue. Our approach is to find the balance between seizing the opportunities of AI and managing its risk, informed by the conviction that AI should be responsible, safe, secure, and trustworthy, human-centric, reliable, privacy-preserving, and accountable. In recent years, the international community has constructed the building blocks of a global AI governance through, for example, the OECD and the G20 AI principles and the UNESCO recommendation. And states and regions are now implementing them in context, as we do through the European AI Act. Let me make 3 points on interoperability, inclusion, and on transparency. In regard to interoperability, to my mind, the organizing principle for this next phase— it does not mean one rulebook for the world, nor harmonizing away legitimate differences. It means frameworks built in different jurisdictions, built on the common international standards to rights, safety, transparency, and accountability. We can recognize and work together with each other instead of fragmenting into patchworks that no one can navigate, but always on the shared global foundation, the UN Charter and international law, including human rights law. Second, inclusion, because the theme is benefit for all. If governance reflects only a narrow set of perspectives, it cannot be sustainable. AI for all must mean more than access to products. It means using AI to solve local problems in health, education, climate, and food. And it deals with the question of who's sitting at the table. AI governance cannot be written by governments or technology companies alone. Civil society, researchers, and the technical community bring knowledge that we lack. And it's our task to give this multi-stakeholder real seats at the real table. Then transparency in practice. Open data, open source, and transparency across the lifecycle foster accountability and let citizens see how these systems affect their lives. Our public algorithm register now documents around 1,500 algorithms across nearly 350 public sector bodies. An example we offer not as an answer, but as something someone can adapt. Colleagues, 2 tasks. Let us treat interoperability as a shared objective, frameworks that work together by default while respecting that approaches differ. And let us build capacity and Global South participation in from the start so that we can agree that reflects the world and the whole world that we live under it. Let me close by underlining the value of a multilateral and above all multi-stakeholder cooperation. and the foundational importance of a rule-based international order. The Netherlands is a committed partner in that work. Thank you.

I thank the Honorable Minister of ICT of Namibia. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, we will have to conclude this high-level governmental plenary segment now. Thank you very much indeed, Ambassadors, Doreen. Thank you all. Thank you, everybody, for a hugely stimulating and engaging few days. I say it feels very— it feels like very much longer already, and let me assure you that that is in an entirely good way, because it has been so packed full of content, of stimulating ideas, and of commitments to, as the speakers just now said, to make sure that this Dialogue carries forward with concrete conversations, with specific ideas, and takes us sets us well onto the road for the second global dialogue. Brace yourselves to be held in New York next May. I'm absolutely delighted to begin this next segment, the dialogue of dialogues, which will start to chart the way for. Forward and think about how the UN can play a key role in ensuring that AI governance is built upon the foundations of human rights and of the values espoused by the UN. I'm delighted to begin with high-level opening remarks, and as befits a multi-stakeholder dialogue, we are delighted to have remarks from different stakeholders here, and I'm beginning— let me begin by welcoming to the stage Her Excellency Halla Tomásdóttir, the President of Iceland. Thank you very much.
I'm here. Excellency.
Nice to meet you. Very warm welcome. Thank you so much.

Thank you so much.

Lovely to see you. Thank you so much. Excellencies, distinguished guests, dear friends, it is an honor to join you for the Global Dialogue on AI Governance. Artificial intelligence is one of the most consequential forces shaping our time.

We all know that. It can improve health, education, food security, disaster preparedness, scientific discovery, and our response to environmental challenges.

But its impacts will not be determined by technological capacity alone.

It will be determined by the human choices we make about. Power, access, accountability, and ultimately the kind of society and humanity we choose to be. Around the world, governments, international institutions, companies, and civil society have put forward important principles for, for artificial intelligence.

Many of them point in the same direction.

Towards safety, inclusion, transparency, accountability, sustainability, and human rights. But we have not yet aligned on shared guardrails, common standards, or the practical accountability that this technology demands.

And principles without practice can inspire false comfort. It is not enough to sound responsible while avoiding the difficult choices that responsibility requires. The central question is not simply how we govern artificial intelligence.

It is whether we can govern ourselves in the age of artificial intelligence. I come from Iceland.

A small island nation that has long turned constraint into creativity. For centuries, we have carried our history, imagination, and values through stories, through the sagas, poetry, music, and our very own language.

They are our roots. They give us a sense of identity, belonging, and continuity across generations.

We have also learned to draw energy from the magma beneath our feet and from the power of our waterfalls, transforming natural forces into warmth, light, and opportunity.

We tend to believe that even the most powerful forces should be put to work for the common good. That, it seems to me, is the test for artificial intelligence as well.

Not simply whether it can create value, but whether it can create shared capability, shared opportunity, and shared prosperity without sacrificing our human dignity, relationships, and sense of— and sense of purpose. Access without agency is not inclusion.

The benefits of AI must reach communities everywhere, not only those already closest to capital, computing power, and decision-making. Those furthest from today's centres of power must be co-authors of this future, with a meaningful role in building the infrastructure, shaping the rules, and sharing fairly in the value created. We should measure success not by the number of pilots we announce, but whether people and communities have greater agency, dignity, and hope because of AI.

AI is not only a technological question. It is a social, economic, and democratic question, and increasingly a question of peace and security. What happens in a world where young people conclude that the safest response to the digital world is to trust nothing and no one? And we must not normalize a future in which human beings delegate the irreversible decision to take a human life to a machine.

Meaningful human responsibility must remain where the stakes our highest. This autumn, Iceland will invite people across the country into a national dialogue in which young people will play a leading role. We need a future-fit leadership that neither confuses speed with progress nor technical capability with wisdom. We need leadership that brings governments, business, educators, researchers, civil society, parents, and young people into genuine partnership. We need leadership that asks not only, what can this technology do, but also, how will it affect the lives of our children?

I come from a country where we have learned to live alongside volcanoes, earthquakes, and pretty unpredictable weather.

Perhaps that is why we tend to believe that powerful forces should be studied, understood, respected, and put to work for the common good.

I believe this is the task before all of us, to ensure that artificial intelligence expands the horizons of young people, of all of us, without diminishing our humanity, to ensure that it helps us become more capable, more creative, more connected, and more hopeful for the future, and to ensure that the intelligence we create remains in the service of the very humanity we share.

Thank you.

Thank you so much, Your Excellency, and thank you for reminding us first that we have key choices to make here— policy choices, individual choices. We're not powerless in the face of technology, but we can choose the path. And secondly, that the path must be guided by the impact on people. That must be the criteria that guides the choices that we make and how we're judged for them. Thank you very much for those powerful remarks. And let me now welcome for our second keynote of this segment, Brad Smith, the Vice Chair and President of Microsoft. You're very welcome.

Well, thank you. It's a real pleasure for me to be here this afternoon. And let me begin where you just left off. We will be measured by the choices we make. And the time to start making them is now, because we come together at what I believe is a critical moment for the future of artificial intelligence. Let's take stock. It was less than 4 years ago, at the end of November in 2022, when ChatGPT was released and in effect a new era with generative AI began. Where are we today? What are the issues we need to address? Well, I think we should start where many of the speakers this afternoon have started as well. Let's look at the state of the world and the divides that characterize the planet on which we live. Let's look at the greatest divide of all, the economic divide between the Global North and South. At Microsoft, one of the things we do is measure every quarter the state of AI diffusion, its usage or adoption on a per capita basis among the working age population in countries around the world. And what we see today is that AI diffusion in the Global North stands at 27%, while in the Global South it is only 15. And what we know is that if current trends persist, by this time next year, AI will be used by more than twice as many people on a per capita basis in the Global North as in the Global South. What does that tell us? It tells us that we are not in good shape. We are not on the right course. And instead, what we are seeing is yet again a new technology trend where digital technology, new technology is going to widen rather than narrow the gap between North and South. We have important decisions to make, and you've heard speakers capture its critical elements. One cannot simply deploy AI in the cloud as if the cloud is the space that it exists. We need a foundation. We need infrastructure. We're trying to invest in that as a company, but we still need to complete the electrification of the world. We have even more distance to travel to complete the internet connectivity of the world. We need to expand the ability of AI models to work equally well in many languages rather than a few. And we need to make digital skilling an everyday reality. Rather than a dream that is being realized by far too few. These are the kinds of steps we need to take, and we need to start by recognizing that we're going to need to bend the arc of history if we're going to make progress. Similarly, I think we need to take stock and acknowledge that around the world—not everywhere—but in many countries, many people have. many more questions and even concerns today than they did just a year ago. They ask, will AI bring me and my family, my neighbors in my community, more economic opportunity or less? Will it create better jobs for my children, or will it instead create technology that creates the jobs we already have? This is not a decision that machines will make. It is a decision that people and governments and countries will make. And we need to make them with the right kind of forethought and the right kind of values if we are going to ensure that AI serves its purpose and creates a better world. And then finally, I think there is in some ways the most fundamental question of all. Where are we when we look at the state of AI governance around the world? I think what we can say is this: over the last 12 months, AI has raced forward and AI governance has not kept pace. We've reached a point of recognizing quite rightly that if not governed well, the risks of AI can grow as they are this year with respect to cybersecurity. As they will in future years when it comes to biology, with technology that can do both enormous good as a tool, but enormous damage as a weapon. We have to catch up. And as you've heard other speakers talk today, there are— there is only one way to catch up when it comes to AI governance. We must work together. We do need an approach that is inclusive, that makes room for every government in the world, as well as multi-stakeholder conversations as we're happening right now today. These are not challenges that can be met by any one sector of the economy alone. Government cannot act alone. The private sector cannot act alone. The nonprofit and NGO sector cannot act alone. But if we act together, we can do better. And as you've heard, we need interoperability. We need to recognize that different countries and cultures will quite rightly exercise their sovereignty and make different choices. That is something that is always part of international relations. But as you've heard, we cannot afford a patchwork that is impossible for people or companies or governments to navigate. We need to build the interoperability among governance systems if we're going to turn the current stalemate into progress. That requires the United Nations. It requires other institutions as well, and there will be many. But I continue to believe that the United Nations, the ITU, the other agencies that are here this weekend, every day of every week, have an indispensable role to play. Only by harnessing the power to bring people together, to solve problems through stronger public policy, to deliver real results through real programs to countries around the world, can we offer what the world needs and what the world deserves: hope. Hope. That we can turn AI into what it should be, a new technology that can build a better world. Certainly on behalf of Microsoft, on behalf of, I think, so many people who come from so many different sections of society and so many parts of the world, I am happy to be here. I am happy that all of you are here, and I am happy that we now have the opportunity to go forward together. Thank you very much.

Thank you so much to Brad Smith for reminding us that while there are many divides here— digital divides, governance divides— it's absolutely critical that we bridge those, that we bridge those through institutions, and that we bridge those through what is rapidly becoming one of my favorite words of the weak interoperability of approaches. For our final plenary segment, for our final keynote speaker of this segment, I'm very delighted to now welcome Mr. Ramanjit Singh Chima, who is the Global Program Director at the Association for Progressive Communications. You're welcome.

Thank you, Thank you so much, Claire. I also wanted to thank the joint organizing team of the AI Dialogue and the agencies who've been working so hard for these conversations here in Geneva and online this week. Your Excellencies, colleagues, I speak to you on behalf of the Association for Progressive Communications. For those of you who may not know us, we are an international nonprofit organization born in 1990 with over 74 organizational members and 44 associates across 60 countries. From the beginning of our existence, APC's network has recognized that it is crucial for the international system to engage with civil society, public interest technologists, and grassroots communities on the design and conversation around technological systems, their development, and governance. And I stand before you today sharing the fact that I feel a bit uneasy. It would be tempting for us here to focus on conversations about the future. How should we approach AI and its governance? But it's rare to find a truly blank slate. The development around AI and its governance, and architectures in particular on institutional development, come from histories that we must learn from. We must not forget that the development of AI is not inevitable, and indeed not as a new phenomenon. As many of you might be aware, AI and the range of technologies that constitute artificial intelligence and the the term we use today, come from development and development cycles of AI booms, or what sometimes people call AI springs and AI winters. What might be, of course, particularly different and unique about today's boom or today's AI spring is the fact that the extent to which it's impacting our communities and societies, that is not merely in labs, in testing environments, and more. And in that context, it is impacting vulnerable communities and individuals And it's already trying to seek and in fact successfully achieves the attention of already strained and contested policy and governance institutions. The internet has become a mainstream force. That does not mean it's universally accessible or it's equitable in its development or in its applications. This is the problem that our communities were engaging, and this is a problem that we need to be honest about when it comes to this space. We were still working hard on getting digital governance right. And we are now under tremendous pressure to leapfrog into a conversation around AI governance and to create effective architectures for it. Global digital governance processes, including those born out of the World Summit for the Information Society, and that includes the UN IGF as well as the processes in the UNCSTD, has demonstrated the value of sustained cross-forum engagement. When we have seen success in digital cooperation at the global level, That has been when governments, civil society, the technical community, academia, the private sector, and international organizations have worked together. Many of those who work for the ITU and other UN agencies here in Geneva, as well as those working in New York and other UN hubs, have recognized and learned this through discussion, dialogue, and sometimes active debate and disagreement with civil society and other stakeholders. AI governance should build on that, not replace that. The United Nations system and the different agencies involved in these conversations must remember this as they plan for the next dialogue in New York, as they design commissions and other fora, particularly given the challenges the UN faces at a broader level over the next few months and the reality of the UN's leadership transition and changes. We need to also recognize that the current and upcoming developments around AI raise concerns that intersect with existing concerns around connectivity, human rights, standards, cybersecurity, and digital inclusion. AI systems are not neutral. They are designed and operated in structures that affect— that come from existing inequalities. Women and girls, gender-diverse people, and other marginalized groups are distinctly and disproportionately harmed by the development and use of AI systems and are underrepresented in the conversations around their evolution, design, and governance. The global dialogue on AI governance is an opportunity for governments and decision makers to embed commitments in these affirmations on gender equality from existing digital policy and cooperation processes into the AI governance conversation from the start. You can learn from those mistakes. You can learn from those wins. While the internet impacts and connects to many, much, many, much, many other parts of our societies and economies, we need to recognize that there is still a reality. Your gender, your community identity, your geography, and more impacts what connectivity you get and whether you get connectivity at all. Absence of connectivity impacts your agency and autonomy. You will still have your data scooped up for AI models and are often experimented on in AI deployment, but you cannot voice your demands, you cannot reveal what is happening, and you cannot provide your thoughts on governance. Connectivity efforts are also being impacted by how AI connectivity conversations— sorry, AI infrastructure conversations are grabbing the attention of policymakers and are focusing on particular approaches regarding deployment of compute infrastructure without looking at what communities want. We need a community-centric approach to internet infrastructure and one that recognizes the impact this has on climate change, a topic that the AI dialogue needs to engage with further and needs to connect further with environmental defenders and more. My colleague Rebecca mentioned this earlier today in the conversation around human rights, saying that we need to recognize that the conversations here about communities, that they are not a last-mile policy problem, but communities need to be a first-mile priority and stakeholder. I want to end with a reminder on history. History has taught our communities that do not be afraid of red lines. In particular, we need to be clear about what we deem and enforce as unacceptable when it comes to people's rights, including their rights to their data and privacy, as well as the sustainability of the planet. June, last month, was the 13-year anniversary of the Snowden revelations. It prompted the United Nations and the UN member states to redouble the protection of the right to privacy in a digital age, to drive national reforms around data access, and more. But all of those stand at risk, and surveillance controls, for example, in particular, are completely at risk of being jeopardized due to the current relentless rush for AI tool and usage, for partnerships between the public sector and AI firms, and other efforts to collect and use data in AI systems. We therefore fully agree with the vision that was hinted at by the Secretary-General and by the High Commissioner for Human Rights today. We need regulation guided by human rights, a universal recognition around leaving no space for data collection and AI development without consent. And in closing, I want to thank you all for this opportunity, and in particular note that civil society looks forward to working with everyone in the AI dialogue through collaboration, through challenge, and through imagination. Thank you.

Thank you so much, Rahman, and thank you for reminding us that it's a very long road that brought us here, and there are many interlocking processes that we have to think about, and much history here also of discussion, of debate among many different stakeholders of these issues. Speaking of many different stakeholders' discussion and debate, we're now going to turn to the panel section of this plenary. Let me just welcome our panelists to the stage. If you could all come up on the stage as I call your name, and then we will begin. Let me first welcome Her Excellency Emma Theofilis, Minister of Information and Communications Technology of Namibia. Very warm welcome to you. Let me welcome Guy Ryder, Under-Secretary-General for Policy at the United Nations, Jan Tallinn, the co-founder of the Future of Life Institute, and Gaia Marcus, the director of the Ada Lovelace Institute. A very warm welcome. Everyone has found their seats? Everyone is comfortable? Great. Let us begin. So this is, this is the concluding plenary panel of the inaugural UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance. And as seems appropriate, we are going to start facing forward into the future and think about the next UN Global Dialogue to be held in May of next year in New York, and to think about some of the things that we have learned over the last 2 days, some of the lessons that we will take, and some of the work that needs to be done in order to get us to that next dialogue. So let me start with you, Under-Secretary-General. Um, we've heard over the last few days of many different processes and initiatives, so all of the huge amounts of work that are going on in different combinations and constellations of stakeholders which are contributing incrementally to AI governance. How can the UN help to connect these efforts to achieve the complementarity, the inclusivity, and the interoperability which I think many people in this room would like to see?

Thank you very much for that question. To answer the question and to look forward, as you have just invited us to do, I think it is worth just seeing for a minute how we got here today. It was only in August of last year that our member states decided to convene this dialogue. This dialogue is happening because 193 countries of the world decided that it would be a good idea to come together and have this dialogue. It is important to remember the mandate, not only what its content is, but who it comes from. It gives a particular importance and a particular legitimacy to what we're all doing here together today. And I have to say that I think we deserve to recognize the extraordinary contributions that people have made to making this dialogue work rather successfully. We owe big thanks to our co-chairs who undertook really very intense consultations to get this dialogue off the ground. We got 1,500 written submissions. And of course we have worked very carefully and very closely with the independent scientific panel that we heard report to us yesterday. And we will be getting an outcome document, an outcome from this dialogue to be prepared by the co-chairs in good time. So this dialogue has set us on, I think, an important road. Now what can the UN do to bring things together? It is obviously true that there is an enormous amount of attention and activity taking place internationally around AI issues, some of them here this week in Geneva, not just this dialogue but the AI for Good events, the WISIS events as well. And the point about this is the UN enjoys one unparalleled comparative advantage in the task before us, and that is the legitimacy of its universality. There is nowhere else where 193 member countries can come together in this all-inclusive conversation, and when we say inclusive, of course, it's all our member states, but it's also business, it's also civil society, as we have just heard. We have a challenge, let me be perfectly honest with you, moderator. Inside the UN system, there's a lot going on inside the system. We need to make sure that what happens inside the UN system is coherent, is complementary. We are working hand in hand within the system, and I think what we've seen from the dialogue and the panel this week is good evidence that we are working well on that. But I also think that we are able through the UN to try to reach out to, to connect with those other international processes that will take place. Not universal ones, but different summits that will take place. No doubt the G20, the G7, and others will want to have their say, and I think we can be a reference point in a gathering. And looking forward, I mean, we've heard some very interesting ideas for initiatives arising during the course of our dialogue. We heard our Secretary-General suggests that we have a child safety pledge acted upon. We heard him talk about a transparency initiative. We have just heard the President of Iceland talk about the national dialogue in that country. These are things we have to put together and I am sure there will be many other initiatives and I think bring to this dialogue, which can be, I think, an annual place to come together, and to really take stock of what we're doing and where we need to go. So I think we've made an enormously encouraging start, but it's a start.
Thank you, Under-Secretary-General. And speaking of starts, what for you would success look like— and I should warn all of the other panellists, you're all getting a variation of this question—

what would success look like by the time the Global Dialogue convenes again in New York Well, we will have some things which we think we, with some confidence, we can rely upon. We'll have another report of the International Scientific Panel and we'll be able to chew on what they bring to the table. No doubt other things such as the initiatives I've just mentioned which have been launched at this dialogue this year will be bringing new ideas to the table, but my view is that success will be both maintaining the UN's position, as I have said, as a unique universal convener for dialogue and having the engagement of our member states, also of other stakeholders, to take forward frankly all of the ideas in terms of objectives which have come out rather clearly from this You know, having AI serve humanity— I know these are sounding rather high-level ideas, but to put those into some sort of operational form. And as I say, I think we've both got the commitment of stakeholders and the direction of travel that will help us to move towards progress in that regard.

Thank you so much, Under-Secretary-General. Minister? Let me now turn to you. We heard from you a moment ago, um, delivering your statement. Um, now, as you said, as you said then, as we've heard several times already, uh, this week, countries are moving at different speeds in developing AI governance frameworks. But of course, all of the countries here share an interest, and their people share an interest, in ensuring that AI contributes to sustainable development and to inclusive growth. So from Namibia's perspective, what practical forms of international cooperation, of the kind of debates that the Under-Secretary-General just referred to, are most needed to help countries build the capacities, the institutions, and the partnerships that are required to govern AI effectively and deliver on the promise that we know there is?

Thank you, VP Moderator. And indeed, I concur with the Under-Secretary-General that the convening of this dialogue is a great first step. Every country is grappling with, you know, how to best manage AI because it's inevitable. Nobody can wait. But I think there are 3 concrete steps we can take, one immediate and perhaps one moderate and some long-term. And I think the first one would be looking at helping countries who are, in many instances, grappling with so many other structural issues, especially us from the Global South, to translate these global AI principles into effective national laws and institutions. I think that would be a good foundation for any country to actually know, based on our context, how to handle the AI question. I was listening to one of the AI panel members yesterday who did say that context determines the outcome, and it's true. We have different regions, we have different contexts, so it's only right that we condense those based on the context of each country, whether from the Global South, Global North, or elsewhere. Then I think the second practical moderate approach that we can look at is continuously investing in digital and data infrastructure. The fact of the matter is some countries are still grappling with getting their citizens digitally literate. It's no secret. To pretend that all of us are at some level the same is not true. We must find a way to create or avail financing to countries that are still teaching their citizens how to trust technology, how to trust the ability to use technology in public service and otherwise, and then continuously elevate from there. Then finally, the long-term would be creating programs to strengthen skills and scientific capacity. From a Namibian perspective of a country on the African continent, it's no secret that almost half of the world's population will come from the African continent. By the year 2050. This means that we have not only the energy and agility of a young population, but we will have the numbers. It's only right that, especially for the Global South and the developing nations, that there are programs tailor-made to train human capacity and human capabilities to strengthen skills and scientific capacity in the Global South.

Thank you, Minister. And let me also ask you the same question that I asked the Under-Secretary-General. This is a huge agenda that you have posed and one that is the work of many people in many years. Practically speaking, what would you like to see by the time we get to the 2nd Global Dialogue? We are perhaps sitting, if we're invited back, on another panel like this. What would you like to see? What would success look like? How would you know that we were moving forward?

Well, the next one will be 10 months from now, so there's a lot of work to do in less than a year. But I think success in May 2027 in New York would look like, one, having a shared but flexible reference framework for AI governance. I say flexible again, as I've spoken about the context earlier before. And this reflects on all the regions across the world and giving countries like ours, small states, developing states like Namibia, where I'm from, a practical but sovereign template for national legislation and, of course, our institutions. The second one would be visible capacity gains in the Global South. Like I said with the example earlier before, we need more trained regulators. We need more national AI strategies. Deployed and more cross-regional AI initiatives advancing inclusive growth and resilience, especially for countries that are compounded with AI coming up, but they do not necessarily have the capacity in-country so that there's no dependence on other people's capabilities for one's own country. Last, reflecting on Goal 17, would be partnerships, global partnerships around this dialogue, where governments, industry, academia, civil society are regularly exchanging evidence, updating norms, and co-developing open tools that we can use in administrating the use of AI for now and the future, and that the voices of some are not lesser than others. I'm a government representative, but many instances we depend on all these actors to properly advise policymakers such as myself to genuinely take a listening ear to actually put the necessary safeguards in place to protect citizens. This is, I think, what success would look like in the next 10 months before we meet in New York in May.

Thank you. Thank you. That is, as you say, a big agenda for 10 months. I don't want to quash your applause, please. And I'm very glad that you raised the question of partnerships. I've already heard many announcements of very exciting new partnerships, and for those that haven't yet, let me encourage you all to take a look at the Partnerships Hub that has been launched as part of this dialogue. There are some fantastic examples there of exactly what you described, practical coalitions of different stakeholders coming together to solve some of the many— some of the practical problems that have been outlined here today. So it's great to see that, those solutions starting to come. Jan Tallinn, the Future of Life Institute. We've heard, I think, through the dialogue recognition of the, the particular moment that we're in with the, the huge increase in AI's transformative opportunities and capable systems that we, that we are seeing reflected. As you think about that, where, where would you see the greatest need for international cooperation in the face of this rapidly developing industry.

Thank you very much. Indeed, I think it's great to see this kind of awareness throughout the dialogue and like indeed in the world that finally AI is becoming very capable. I certainly see it in my own, own field of software development, but clearly healthcare sciences, there's so much good that can be done with AI. But I think even the best experts are only now starting to grasp that the progress will actually accelerate from here. The big reason is that the top AI companies are now openly pursuing what's known as recursive self-improvement, that is, using their own AI to accelerate the development of AI. Just yesterday, uh, Jack Clark, co-founder of Anthropic, said that their top model now did a new world record in in one of the crucial tasks of machine learning, the GPU kernel development. Now the problem with this recursive self-improvement is that you're risking losing the control because you're giving machines more and more autonomy. And the autonomy that makes those— more generally, the autonomy that makes these systems useful is also what makes it— makes them harder to control. As the Secretary-General said, these systems are actually no longer tools awaiting instruction, and our intuitions and institutions are not ready for machines that decide. And in the worst case, we indeed lose control altogether. And as the panel's report makes it clear, reliable methods for retaining control over highly autonomous AI systems are lacking. But of course, that's not inevitable. The choice, as Secretary-General puts it, is between governing by design and drifting by default— probably drifting in the, in the wind of economic pressure. But in the end, it is the path that we humanity are choosing, and we can choose a better path. Because the reason why we are rushing towards these dangerous thresholds is because of the competitive dynamics driving this AI development. And indeed, even the, the leaders of the top AI companies now are, are voicing the caution. They are saying that they would like to slow down, but they really can't because of this commercial and geopolitical pressure. And this is where UN and more, more generally international cooperation can step in to make sure that there is like international pressure to progress at a safe pace so we can actually capture the AI benefits, the increasing capabilities that the increasing capabilities are bringing, and not kind of succumb to this loss of control that's driven by the race. And I think with this dialogue and the scientific panels, independent evidence. The UN, obviously, as the most legitimate organization on the planet, is uniquely placed to build that cooperation.

Thank you. Thank you, Jan. And looking ahead to the next dialogue, we've heard that there are many risks ahead, and particularly, as you've just said, with the developments in the technology, but we've also heard throughout the last few days excitement about innovation and opportunity. How do you think that we should be collectively prioritizing to anticipate those risks, but while also supporting the innovation that we want?

So I think it's— again, it's great to have this report because it's easy to just look at it. And, and say that the report points like several key problems that we, that we're going to face. One is that, as I already mentioned, AI capabilities are advancing faster than our ability to govern them. Second, the companies now actually have the highest level of knowledge. They know more, far more about how capable and how safe their systems are really than the governments and the public. And the third which is like now becoming very clear. Most countries, including many advanced economies, lack the technical expertise to assess the most capable AI or have a real say in governing it. And because these risks are actually cross-borders, even if you don't have a say, you're still going to be subject to the risks. The countries left out are exposed just like everyone else. So kind of bridging the AI divide and governing the risks are not 2 separate agendas. They're one. I think there's like one way of putting it is that there's like 2 frontiers that are being pushed. One is making AIs more and more capable, and that's kind of happening behind 2 gates. One is what the AI companies are deciding to release, and the other is what the host country is kind of enabling. enabling the rest of the world to access. And even the companies themselves, as I mentioned, are kind of trying to go like, help us, let's, let's be more careful here. And the other frontier is basically the AI adoption, diffusion, and actually putting the capabilities into good use. So there is really no dilemma anymore between— dichotomy between innovation and safety, because most of the safety concerns are in the first frontier. where the companies are racing into unknown. And most of the innovation and benefits actually come from the second frontier, where the companies can— companies and communities in general can actually tap into those capabilities.

Thank you very much. And in the spirit of the Dialogue of Dialogues, the title of this session, I think, you know, bringing what you have said together together about the fact that these different issues, although they may sometimes be discussed in different fora, are not at all in contradiction with each other, and Under-Secretary-General Ryder's comment about the UN being the inclusive forum where these things can come together. I think, again, this speaks very much to what we are all doing in this room today and the value of this forum, so thank you for that. Gaia, coming to you last. Gaia Markus, the Director of the Ada Lovelace Institute. We've heard, I think, already from several panellists, from Her Excellency the President of Iceland earlier, the critical importance of inclusion, of public trust, and that has been a recurring theme across the different cluster conversations that have been happening in these rooms. What practical mechanisms do you think can, can help to ensure that the diverse voices that we need continue to shape AI governance between these 2 dialogues and beyond?

Thank you. It is truly an honor to be addressing you all today. In reflecting what we have heard, it strikes me that we cannot understate how historic it is that all UN member states now have a seat at the AI table. And inclusion cannot stop at the level of states. For this dialogue to be legitimate, we need to move from hearing only about the futures that a few companies, investors, or powerful actors want to see, as we have heard, to hearing the hopes, aspirations, and fears of people around the globe as AI becomes intertwined with everyday life. So embedding trust and inclusion into this dialogue cannot mean treating participation as a side event or a consultation exercise. Trust is built through reliability, responsiveness, integrity, fairness, openness, and above all accountability. And these are qualities of the governance process itself. So the question becomes, how do we make sure that diverse voices are not just heard, but they truly shape decisions between Geneva and New York in 2027 and then far beyond. So there are 2 things that we would like to see, to see trust and inclusion really sit as the bedrock of this dialogue. First, we need to treat public participation as a source of evidence. Global AI governance should be shared, as we know, by a shared understanding of evidence, not only the technical evidence about AI systems for evidence about how impacts are being experienced by real people across the world. Scientific evidence is essential, but in AI, consensus can take time, and the evidence often lags behind the pace of change. As we heard yesterday, while incredibly laudable in and of itself, the independent scientific panel gives us the floor of our concern. Not the ceiling. And while our focus must be on human rights-protecting, safe, and trusted AI for all, it is often the people most affected by these technologies that are the true experts in their impacts. Workers really understand the effects and implications of automation. The most vulnerable— women, girls, children— bring lived experience of the hard edges of technologies that are deployed before they are governed and deployed before they are safe. So second, to know that we're making progress on inclusive and trusted AI, participation needs clear docking points into institutions and power. Inclusion of marginalized people and of those who have the most to gain from AI will not automatically lead to trust, and it will not lead to change unless their experiences and expectations are connected to clear levers of power. That means the dialogue must be the place where different mechanisms, be they a citizens' track of affected communities, national and regional dialogues, or participatory incident reporting mechanisms— the dialogue must be the place where these mechanisms contribute to outcomes that have clear accountability. Participation does not just mean collecting or representing views, but making sure that those views shape agendas, evidence priorities, and recommendations. So now, now I'd say is a moment for courage, not a moment to stand in beautiful contemplation of the various problems that we are all aware of. We need to move forward with a shared expectation that this dialogue can set a global AI governance floor with clarity on what is and what isn't acceptable, with respect for the rule of law and with the full spectrum of international human rights as its foundation. So for 2027, we need to act decisively, developing an embedded and institutionalized participation architecture around the dialogue that adds substance to a recognized, respected, and defended global governance floor, a floor that complements existing processes processes, but adds a shared global layer, a floor that recognizes lived experience as evidence, gives communities clear routes into decision-making, and creates transparent obligations that the dialogue is accountable for. That is how inclusion moves from being a theme to becoming a governance mechanism, and how public trust becomes something that is earned, not something that is simply asserted. Thank you,

Gaia. Thank you so much. I mean, we've heard from all of you, I think, some recurrent themes and also some very strong directions for the next dialogue. We've heard of the need for a flexible framework, one that can accommodate the rapid changes in technology, the rapid changes in the needs of different countries and communities, and the rapidly evolving field of AI governance itself. We've heard of the need for an inclusive approach, inclusive of all UN member states and inclusive of communities and of those voices that often are not heard in these debates, and of course inclusive of the companies who are developing AI and bringing it through the products to— into people's hands. We've also heard about the need for governance to have a practical application, for the, the link of a— the link from a broad AI governance conversation to national implementation, to practical changes in people's lives, and of the need to link up the conversations that are happening around the world, whether those be thematic in terms of addressing specific parts of the agenda— safety, innovation, and so on— or whether they be the conversations that are happening in different fora where not all are represented, although progress and new ideas can be made. So we need, I think, to recognize, as Under-Secretary-General Bill Ryder said, the critical role here of the UN as the place where all of these different attributes of dialogue can come together. We have a few more minutes, I think, of the panel, so I would like to ask all of you one final wrap-up question. As you have been listening to the conversations, participating in panels, having your— I'm sure your many bilateral conversations over the last few days. What do you think, as we approach the final sessions of this dialogue, what in— well, it says in my script in one word, I might allow you 3 or 4. What do you hope is carried forward when— from here, from Geneva to New York, when we meet again in May 2027? Let me just start with you, Minister, and go down the row. Thank you
so much, Clare. I think for me, the immediate word that comes to mind is equity, but another couple of words that come to mind is collective progress. So equity and collective progress. Thank you.
Thank you. Guy?

I certainly agree with both of those ideas. But it seems to me from the conversation, you know, that if we are successful in what we are trying to do, advance on the 3 sort of lines of action which actually flow from the Global Digital Compact, which, you know, gave birth to this dialogue, we need to advance on the governance discussion. It doesn't mean we'll have a fully fledged agreement around governance, but the parameters of the things we need to do around governance.
